question: If our own wrong guesses make AI agents fail, how should we learn to give them better instructions?
reflection: Working well with machines starts with knowing the limits of our own knowledge, which is a skill that helps us everywhere.

sources.subject: Claude's crypto breakthrough + AI's $3 trillion debt problem
DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, Anthropic OSS Scanner, DeepMind Agent Study

one_line: AI agents are getting more capable, but research suggests the human giving them instructions is now a major source of failure, while the money behind the AI build-out looks more fragile.

top_stories.title: Wrong hints from users can halve agent success
top_stories.what: A Google DeepMind study reportedly found that when users give AI agents a mistaken guess about a task, the agents' success rate drops by nearly half.
top_stories.why: This is a human-behaviour problem at the centre of AI adoption, and training staff in how to brief AI tools is a clear behavioural-science service.

top_stories.title: AI infrastructure debt worries investors
top_stories.what: AI-linked borrowers reportedly carry more than $3 trillion in debt, and lenders now demand much higher returns from some cloud providers, such as CoreWeave.
top_stories.why: If cheap AI capacity depends on fragile debt, organisations should avoid locking long projects to a single small provider.

top_stories.title: Anthropic points its AI at security problems
top_stories.what: Anthropic launched a free scanner that reportedly found hundreds of serious bugs in open-source projects in a week, and says a Claude research model explained the origin of seeds behind widely used encryption curves.
top_stories.why: AI-driven security checks are becoming cheap enough for small teams and public bodies that rely on open-source software.

saudi_lens.text: As Saudi government services roll out AI agents, the quality of staff instructions may matter as much as the model, so prompt and briefing training belongs in digital upskilling programmes.

idea.title: Briefing the machine
idea.pitch: A field experiment comparing staff who get a short training on how to brief AI agents with staff who do not, measuring task success and time saved.
idea.first_step: Pick one routine task done with an AI tool and write a one-page briefing checklist to test.
